name: Lysippos of Sikyon
period: About 390–305 BCE
availability: Contemporary model; travel, patronage and a specific encounter would need separate authored content.
contribution: Signed statue bases preserve his authorship even where the bronze has vanished. Supports credited commissions, workshop practice and a body of work; reported production totals are not a measured game target.

name: Eutychides of Sikyon
period: Active around 300 BCE
availability: Later-career contemporary model, around age 50 for the starting cohort; no meeting is implemented.
contribution: The Tyche of Antioch connects a civic commission with local topography and an image reproduced by later artists. Supports a designed public work and its later use, without taking credit for the historical statue.

name: Chares of Lindos
period: Early third century BCE; Colossus dated 295–283 BCE in Badoud's reconstruction
availability: Late-life model, roughly ages 55–67; construction dates and technical reconstruction require care.
contribution: The Colossus of Rhodes offers a model for a large civic bronze requiring planning, resources and completion. The monument is lost and its reconstruction remains debated; the player does not automatically build a historical Wonder.

name: Xenocrates of Chalcedon
period: About 396/395–314/313 BCE; Academy head from 339/338 BCE
availability: Contemporary school model; the real Academy's succession is not reassigned to the player.
contribution: Sustained leadership of a philosophical school supports teaching, institutional continuity and succession distinct from family inheritance. Accounts of his selection differ, and his own writings are lost.

name: Epicurus
period: 341–270 BCE; Garden established in Athens in 306 BCE
availability: Later-career contemporary model; the Garden begins around player age 44.
contribution: A connected philosophical system, practical exercises and a continuing community support an independent school route. The player's inquiry keeps its own name and need not reproduce Epicurus's doctrines.

name: Zeno of Citium
period: Stoic school founded around 300 BCE
availability: Later-career contemporary model, around player age 50; no direct discipleship is implemented.
contribution: Study across several traditions followed by a school of his own supports defended argument and independent teaching. Stoic physics, logic and ethics illustrate connected inquiry rather than a single proficiency test.

name: Pytheas of Massalia
period: Fourth century BCE; expedition dates uncertain
availability: Contemporary reference model; uncertain biography does not establish a fixed meeting window.
contribution: An account describing Britain supports observation, sailing reports and later scrutiny. His work survives through other authors; the exact northern itinerary and the location of Thule must remain uncertain.

name: Androsthenes of Thasos
period: Fleet service in 326 BCE; Arabian coastal exploration in 324 BCE
availability: Contemporary expedition model, around player ages 24–26; actual participation would require a travel and service record.
contribution: Fleet service followed by exploration of Bahrain and the Arabian coast supports a survey and observational report alongside a command route. His account informed later geographical and botanical writing.

name: Patrocles
period: Active after 312 BCE; Caspian expedition around 285 BCE
availability: Late-life model, around player age 65 for the Caspian expedition; suitable for future later-generation content too.
contribution: A command career led to geographical exploration, but his reports also supported mistaken conclusions about the Caspian and rivers. Reward a completed survey separately from an unverified claim about the wider world.

name: Craterus
period: Late fourth century BCE; Alexander's campaigns and the successor wars
availability: Contemporary command model; disputed successor-war chronology is not converted into a new encounter date.
contribution: Independent responsibilities included forces, supplies and the return of veterans. Supports bounded command duties and logistics rather than counting victories alone; a successful career can still end in defeat.

name: Coenus
period: Hyphasis refusal to advance, 326 BCE
availability: Contemporary campaign model, around player age 24; no campaign participation is inferred from reading the reference.
contribution: Arrian presents Coenus speaking for exhausted soldiers when Alexander wished to advance. Supports judgement, cohesion and a reasoned refusal; the episode is not a battlefield defeat or a guaranteed reward for dissent.

name: Phocion
period: Fourth century BCE; Athenian command and political reversals
availability: Contemporary civic and military model; Athenian office still requires its own eligibility and appointment.
contribution: Plutarch's life connects repeated command with civic decisions, removal and execution, followed by later rehabilitation. Supports separating a record of service from current office and changing public reputation; the biography has a moralizing perspective.

name: Herakleides of Salamis
period: Grain deliveries and contributions in 330/329 and 328/327 BCE; honours in 325/324 BCE
availability: Contemporary commercial model, around player ages 20–26; the documented Athenian honours belong to Herakleides.
contribution: Public decrees record supplied grain, financial help and civic recognition, while also describing interference with his voyage. Supports fulfilled obligations, transport risk and reputation built through repeated useful trade.

name: Cleomenes of Naucratis
period: Egyptian administration under Alexander, late fourth century BCE
availability: Contemporary fiscal and grain-trade model; an official appointment is distinct from a trading distinction.
contribution: Accounts of his revenue management and grain policies support conflicts among profit, public supply and political accountability. Modern source criticism cautions that hostile reports may serve political interests; allegations are not treated as neutral measurements.

name: Zenon of Kaunos
period: Archive begins in 261 BCE; estate management in 256–248 BCE
availability: Later-generation reference, ages 89+ for the starting cohort; playable descendants are not implemented by this feature.
contribution: A dated documentary archive traces service, correspondence, estate management and dismissal. Supports accounts, receipts, delegated responsibility and career reversals without turning every archive document into Zenon's personal achievement.

name: Callippus of Cyzicus
period: Fourth century BCE
availability: Contemporary intellectual model; the reference supplies no fixed meeting or appointment.
contribution: Aristotle describes Callippus revising Eudoxus's sphere models to account for observed motions. Supports comparison, criticism and a revised explanatory model, while keeping historical models separate from modern astronomical truth.

name: Autolycus of Pitane
period: About 360–290 BCE; dates uncertain
availability: Contemporary mathematical-astronomy model, including the cohort's middle and later career.
contribution: Surviving works on the moving sphere and risings and settings connect demonstrated geometry with astronomy. Supports reproducible exposition without requiring a famous mentor; priority and dependence claims involving Euclid remain disputed.

name: Aristarchus of Samos
period: About 310–230 BCE; active in the early third century BCE
availability: Late-life or later-generation model; flourishing around 280–260 BCE corresponds to player ages 70–90.
contribution: Geometrical reasoning about celestial distances and a separately reported heliocentric hypothesis support bold explanations with explicit observational limits. His surviving distance treatise is not heliocentric, and no earlier encounter is invented.

name: Timotheus of Thebes
period: Alexander's court; Susa wedding performances in 324 BCE
availability: Contemporary performance model, around player age 26; distinguish him from Timotheus of Miletus.
contribution: Traditions place this aulos player at court and with choral performance. Supports preparation for a demanding engagement and coordination with others; stories about music instantly controlling Alexander are rhetorical anecdotes, not reliable mechanics.

name: Aristoxenus of Tarentum
period: Born about 370 BCE; nothing securely known of his life after 322 BCE
availability: Contemporary musical and philosophical model; an unknown death date is not permission for unlimited direct teaching.
contribution: Musical writing, training and study at Aristotle's Lyceum support a route through careful listening, explanation and teaching. His institutional ambitions also show that expertise does not itself secure a school's leadership.

name: Satyra
period: Documented in 258–257 BCE
availability: Later-generation reference, around player ages 92–93; no contemporary mentor encounter is added.
contribution: A dated linen account names Satyra as a kitharode. This sparse documentary trace supports the presence of a named female professional performer, without supplying a full biography or proving an otherwise undocumented touring career.
